question: A busbar in an aircraft electrical system is:

options.text: A device that converts the generator output from AC to DC
A protective device that disconnects a circuit on overload
A common conductor that distributes power from sources to many circuits
The earth-return path formed by the airframe structure

explanation: Sources (generators, battery, TRUs, external power) feed busbars; loads are fed from the busbars through their own protection. Grouping loads on separate busbars by importance is what makes load shedding and fault isolation possible.

question: In a single-pole (earth-return) DC distribution system:

options.text: Only one load at a time can be connected to the bus
The metal structure is the return conductor, saving return wires
The negative side of the battery is left unconnected to the structure
Every load has both a supply wire and a separate insulated return wire

explanation: The negative terminal of the battery and generators is bonded to the airframe, and each load is earthed locally. Only one wire per circuit is needed — a large weight saving — but a chafed supply wire touching structure becomes a short circuit.

question: Two-wire (double-pole) circuits are used in preference to earth return near the aircraft's magnetic compass because:

options.text: A two-wire circuit carries less current than an earth-return circuit for the same load
Earth-return currents cannot flow through the structure near the compass
Two-wire circuits are lighter than earth-return circuits
Side-by-side supply and return currents have fields that largely cancel

explanation: A current flowing through the structure can follow an unpredictable path and create a magnetic field near the compass. Running the return alongside the supply makes the two fields nearly cancel. Two-wire systems are also needed on non-conducting composite structures.

question: On an aircraft with a largely composite (non-metallic) structure, an earth-return system:

options.text: Is unnecessary, because composite aircraft use only AC power
Is provided automatically by the carbon fibres, which conduct as well as aluminium
Needs dedicated return conductors or an added conductive network
Works better than on a metal aircraft, because composites have lower resistance

explanation: Fibreglass does not conduct, and carbon fibre conducts far less well than aluminium and unevenly. Composite aircraft therefore carry return wiring or an embedded current-return network, and also need special provision for lightning protection and bonding.

question: Electrical loads in an aircraft are grouped onto separate busbars (essential, main, non-essential) so that:

options.text: Each load can be supplied at a different voltage
No circuit protection is needed on the essential busbar
Less important loads can be shed if generation is lost
The total current drawn from the generators is always the same

explanation: With a generator failure or on battery alone, there is not enough power for everything. Disconnecting the non-essential (and sometimes main) buses — automatically or by the crew — protects the supply to flight-critical equipment.

question: An essential busbar is sometimes supplied from two sources through diodes. The purpose of the diodes is to:

options.text: Convert the AC from each source into DC for the bus
Let either source feed the bus without feeding back into the other
Reduce the bus voltage to a level safe for avionics
Ensure only the first source to come on line can ever supply the bus

explanation: Each diode conducts only from its source towards the bus. Whichever source has the higher voltage supplies the bus; a failed source cannot drag the bus down or draw current from the other one.

question: An ammeter is connected:

options.text: In series with the circuit, and has a very high internal resistance
In parallel with the circuit, and has a very low internal resistance
In parallel with the circuit, and has a very high internal resistance
In series with the circuit, and has a very low internal resistance

explanation: An ammeter must carry the circuit current, so it goes in series, and it must disturb that current as little as possible, so its resistance is very low. A voltmeter is the opposite: in parallel, with very high resistance.

question: A voltmeter is connected:

options.text: In parallel with the component, and has a very low internal resistance
In series with the component, and has a very high internal resistance
In series with the component, and has a very low internal resistance
In parallel with the component, and has a very high internal resistance

explanation: A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points, so it is connected across them. A high resistance means it draws almost no current and does not alter the voltage it is measuring.

question: An ammeter is mistakenly connected directly across (in parallel with) a 28 V supply. The likely result is:

options.text: A correct reading of the current drawn by the circuit
A very large current through the meter, damaging it or blowing the circuit protection
A reading of the supply voltage in volts
A reading of zero, because no current can flow through an ammeter in parallel

explanation: With its very low resistance, an ammeter across the supply is effectively a short circuit. Wrongly connecting a voltmeter in series, by contrast, does no damage: its high resistance simply stops the load working while the meter reads close to the supply voltage.

question: A shunt is used with an ammeter that must measure large currents. The shunt is:

options.text: A low-resistance conductor; the meter reads the voltage drop across it
A high-resistance coil in series with the meter, limiting its current
A transformer that steps the current down before it reaches the meter
A capacitor across the meter that smooths the reading

explanation: The heavy current flows through the shunt; the meter, connected across it, sees a few millivolts proportional to that current and is calibrated in amps. Only a tiny current passes through the instrument itself.

question: A centre-zero ammeter in the battery line of a light aircraft shows a reading to the negative side in flight. This indicates that:

options.text: The ammeter has failed, since a battery cannot discharge in flight
The battery is being charged by the alternator
The alternator is supplying all the loads and the battery is fully charged
The battery is discharging, supplying current to the aircraft's loads

explanation: A centre-zero ammeter shows the direction of current: plus for charging, minus for discharging. A discharge in flight means the alternator is not carrying the load — failed, or overloaded — and the battery is being run down.

question: A loadmeter, as opposed to a centre-zero ammeter, is connected in the generator output and indicates:

options.text: The generator's output current, often as a fraction of its rating
The frequency of the generator output
The voltage of the busbar the generator is connected to
Whether the battery is charging or discharging

explanation: A loadmeter reads from zero upward only, since a generator should never pass reverse current. A reading of 0.6 means the generator is carrying 60% of its rated load — useful for checking load sharing and for load management after a failure.

question: A loadmeter on a 300 A generator reads 0.75. The generator is supplying:
explanation: A loadmeter graduated in fractions of rated load reads 0.75 × 300 A = 225 A.

question: A DC external power receptacle is often fitted with a short pin that energises the external power relay. Its purpose is to ensure that:

options.text: The relay makes after, and breaks before, the main pins, so they never arc
The external power is connected only when the aircraft battery is flat
The external power unit is switched off automatically after a set time
The aircraft can be supplied from two ground power units at once

explanation: The short control pin is the last to make and the first to break. The heavy current is therefore always switched by the relay's contacts, never by the plug being pushed in or pulled out under load.

question: A ground power unit is connected to a DC aircraft with its polarity reversed. A typical aircraft protection is that:

options.text: The aircraft battery automatically reverses its own polarity to match
The external power relay will not close, so the reversed supply never reaches the bus
The bus is supplied normally, since DC equipment works with either polarity
The external power relay closes and the battery fuse blows to protect the aircraft

explanation: Reversed polarity could destroy electronic equipment and drive a large current into the battery. A diode in the relay coil circuit (or a polarity-sensing unit) lets the relay operate only when the polarity is correct.

question: Many light aircraft have an avionics master switch. Its main purpose is to:

options.text: Increase the voltage supplied to the avionics during engine start
Act as a circuit breaker for all avionics with a single reset
Keep the avionics off during engine start, away from voltage transients
Allow the avionics to be supplied by the alternator only, never the battery

explanation: Starter engagement and disengagement cause voltage dips and spikes on the bus. Switching the radios on only after the start (and off before shutdown) protects them, and gives a single switch to remove all avionics load in an electrical emergency.

question: A split master switch in a light aircraft has battery (BAT) and alternator (ALT) halves. It is generally arranged so that:

options.text: The ALT half can be switched off on its own, but switching the BAT half off also takes the ALT half off
The BAT half can be switched off on its own while the alternator continues to supply the bus
Both halves always move together and cannot be operated separately
The ALT half must be switched on before the BAT half for the battery to connect

explanation: Taking the alternator off line alone is a standard response to an overvoltage or a faulty alternator. Running the alternator without the battery is avoided because the battery helps stabilise the bus voltage and the alternator field normally depends on it.

question: Cables carrying heavy currents over long runs are made of a larger cross-section mainly to:

options.text: Limit the voltage drop along the cable and the heat generated in it
Reduce the cable's inductance so that it can be used on AC
Allow the use of a smaller circuit breaker
Increase the voltage at the far end above the source voltage

explanation: The cable's resistance causes a voltage drop (IR) and heating (I²R). A bigger section lowers the resistance, so the load receives its rated voltage and the cable stays within its temperature limit. Long runs need bigger cables for the same current.

question: Under the American Wire Gauge (AWG) system used for aircraft cables, a larger gauge number indicates:

options.text: A greater number of strands of the same total cross-section
A higher insulation voltage rating, independent of conductor size
A smaller conductor cross-section, able to carry less current
A larger conductor cross-section, able to carry more current

explanation: AWG numbers run backwards: a 22 AWG wire is thin and used for signals, while 2 AWG or 0 AWG cables carry the heavy currents of a battery or starter.

question: Automatic load shedding in a DC system typically:

options.text: Disconnects the battery from the bus once it is fully charged
Reduces the voltage of the bus to lower the total power consumed
Connects additional generators in parallel when the load exceeds a set value
Drops non-essential loads after a generator failure to avoid overload

explanation: Losing a generator halves (or worse) the available supply. Shedding galley, cabin and other non-essential loads keeps the surviving source within its rating. Crew action may be needed to shed further loads when on battery only.

question: In a split-bus DC system, the left and right buses are each normally supplied by their own generator. If one generator fails:

options.text: A bus tie lets the remaining generator supply both buses, shedding load as needed
The remaining generator doubles its output voltage to supply both buses
Both buses are lost until the failed generator is reset
The battery takes over the failed side permanently, with no bus tie

explanation: Keeping the buses separate in normal operation stops a fault on one side affecting the other. On a generator loss the tie lets the healthy generator feed both, within its rating — which is why load shedding usually accompanies the transfer.

question: Aircraft cables are clamped and routed away from fuel, hydraulic and oxygen lines mainly because:

options.text: The magnetic field of the cable can stop fluids flowing in nearby pipes
Fluid pipes are used as the earth return and must not be touched by cables
Chafed insulation could arc and ignite leaking fluids or oxygen
Contact with pipes would change the resistance of the cable

explanation: Vibration and movement wear through insulation over time. A resulting arc is an ignition source; near fuel or hydraulic fluid it can start a fire, and near oxygen it can be catastrophic. Separation, clamping and protection sleeves reduce that risk.

question: A busbar voltmeter in a 28 V DC aircraft reads 24 V in flight with the generator switched on. The most likely conclusion is:

options.text: The generator is in an overvoltage condition
The generator is not supplying the bus and the battery is carrying the load
The generator is supplying the bus normally and charging the battery
The battery is being overcharged

explanation: With the generator on line, bus voltage should be at the regulated value of about 28 V. A reading near the battery's own nominal voltage means the battery is the source — the generator has dropped off line, or is not producing enough output.

question: Vital services, such as emergency lighting and the crash-switch operation of the fire extinguishers, are normally supplied from:

options.text: The external power receptacle, through its own relay
The battery (hot) bus, connected directly to the battery
The galley bus, which is shed first after a failure
The non-essential bus, fed only from the generators

explanation: Vital services must work even after a wheels-up landing with every generator stopped and switches off, so they are wired to the bus that is always connected to the battery. Essential services can be fed from generators or batteries; non-essential services come from the generators and are the ones shed.

question: On an aircraft with two DC generators, a differential cut-out connects the second generator to the bus only when its voltage is slightly above the bus voltage. This prevents:

options.text: Circulating current flowing from the bus into the oncoming generator
The first generator being shut down by the second
The battery being overcharged by two generators at once
The bus voltage exceeding the overvoltage limit

explanation: If the oncoming generator were connected at a lower voltage, current would flow into it from the bus — a circulating current that would try to motor it. Waiting until it is a little higher (around 2%) ensures it takes up load straight away.

question: To extend the range of a moving-coil instrument:

options.text: Both use a high-resistance multiplier in series with the meter
Both use a low-resistance shunt in parallel with the meter
An ammeter uses a high-resistance multiplier in series; a voltmeter uses a low-resistance shunt in parallel
An ammeter uses a low-resistance shunt in parallel; a voltmeter uses a high-resistance multiplier in series

explanation: A shunt bypasses most of a large current around the delicate coil; a multiplier limits the current through the coil when it is placed across a high voltage. Either way only a small, proportional current passes through the movement.

question: If the contacts of a DC generator's reverse current cut-out stuck closed after the engine was shut down, the most likely result is:

options.text: No effect, since a stopped generator draws no current
The battery would be overcharged by the generator
The battery would drive current back into the generator, risking burning it out
The generator would continue to charge the battery from its residual magnetism

explanation: With the generator stopped, its EMF is zero, so the battery sees a low-resistance path back through the armature. A large reverse current would flow, flattening the battery and possibly burning out the generator — the very thing the cut-out exists to prevent.
